President Trump's in Shenzhen, China, arriving hours ago to red carpet welcomed by President Xi Jinping.
Trump was to hold direct talks with Xi and according to a White House official who was not authorized to speak on the record with Russian leader Vladimir Putin separately before all three held their historic trilateral talks tomorrow.
We have more on this from NPR's Frank Ordonez.
President Trump landed in China in advance of the high stakes talks with the two leaders on nuclear arms control in the Iran war.
But first the president will meet with his Russian counterpart, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record.
The meeting with Putin was not previously scheduled and the White House has not shared any details about goals for the discussions.
But Trump has said that he wants to speak with Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.
Over the last few weeks, including ahead of the midterms, Trump has been making controversial inroads with Moscow.
He stopped some sanctions and announced a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel fuel.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen appeared in front of members of Congress on Capitol Hill today alongside other top intelligence officials.
They were scheduled to talk about worldwide threats since the 9/11 attacks. But as NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells us, the focus quickly shifted to more recent troubles.
The senior administration officials were questioned about a string of tech outages,
most notably the rare nationwide ground stop that stranded thousands of airline passengers Friday afternoon and into the weekend.
That closely coincided with outages of Microsoft Outlook, major banks and other services.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said that he understood that such notable outages happening at the same time is raising questions from the American public,
but reiterated that they are all separate incidents associated with technical problems.
They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.
The Trump administration has been adamant that the outages are isolated and unconnected.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Washington.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is on track to becoming the first black person to serve as Speaker of the House.
He was nominated today and in January when the next Congress convenes, the full House will vote.
Today, Jeffries said the priority is to bring economic relief and to root out public corruption,
which some polls suggested was an even bigger concern than cost of living when people voted in the midterms.
House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones because the American people deserve better.
The new House Speaker will be tasked with uniting factions within the Democratic majority,
including those elected in more than 50 districts that went for President Trump in 2024.
This is NPR News.
Defense Secretary Pete Heksef says the United States and Venezuela have signed a new deal to reestablish military ties.
Heksef is visiting the South American country as the U.S. seeks to expand its influence in the region,
including access to oil reserves and critical minerals since the U.S. military raid that ousted former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January.
The White House is celebrating historic improvements in confronting drug overdose deaths.
But Trump officials also made misleading claims about who deserves credit for the progress.
Here's NPR's Brian Mann.
In a statement, White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sarah Carter said fatal street drug overdoses are now at their lowest level in nearly a decade.
She suggested the gains have happened over the last 18 months under Trump.
In fact, preliminary data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows the biggest drop in drug deaths happened in 2023 and 2024
when Biden was still in office.
NPR asked the White House about their misleading timeline.
In an email to NPR, Carter said Biden deserves no credit for his administration's fentanyl response.
She blamed Biden for the spike in drug deaths that occurred during the COVID pandemic.
Brian Mann, NPR News.
